newsitem.title: KENYA: Tanzanian report says auctions distorted by reform.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian report says auctions distorted by reform.

text.p: Tanzania's coffee export auctions have been distorted by reforms which allowed multiple licensing for participants, a report in the growth of the industry said on Monday.

"The auction system has lost its meaning. Under the present set-up where a given company has multiple licenses for buying, processing and exporting, auctions become meaningless," said the report obtained by Reuters from Tanzania's agriculture ministry.
"The government should either retain the auctions or abolish multiple licences or introduce a new system," the report added.
Kenyan coffee industry leaders, reacting to the report, said it showed that a rush into reforms could be counter-productive.
"Every single step must be thought out carefully. We need to implement reforms that benefit the farmers, not those that in any way threaten the future," a senior industry official said.
Kenyan millers have pressed for similar licences so they can share the Coffee Board of Kenya's role as a marketing body.
That clamour was silenced at the weekend when President Daniel arap Moi endorsed the board as sole marketing agent.
The report said that the auction system was no longer effective because competition was weakened by companies striving to repossess their own coffee.

"Prices for coffees from (an) exporter who holds the three licences remain artificially low because of weak or no competition at all...Exporters who perform only one function of exporting will be phased out of the market," the report said.

"Prior to liberalisation, there was a clear demarcation between a producer, processor and exporter. Producers were keen to give quality coffee to fetch higher prices at auctions. Processors were neutral entities with no bias in production or export. Exporters were seriously bidding for coffees available at the auction and bidding was effective," the repor said.
The report said liberalising the coffee sector had overemphasised procurement and processing at the expense of production and urged the government to help switch the focus.

It called for production of a massive amount of seedlings to replace ageing trees, improvement in necessary inputs to farmers and revival of dead nationalised coffee farms as important steps in the growth of the coffee industry.
The report said that prior to liberalisation in the 1993/94 (October/September) period, coffee production averaged around 45,000 tonnes against curing capacity of 68,800 tonnes.
But reforms led to the mushrooming of curing factories, with processing capacity rising to 110,400 tonnes when production is steadily declining and could touch 41,000 tonnes in 1996/97.

"All the processing factories are operating below rated capacity. Capacity under-utilisation is a costly phenomenon because it covers the plant, warehousing and workshops. Such costs are passed over to farmers," the report said.
"As a result of capacity under-utilisation in (Tanzania's four) traditional factories, there has been massive retrenchment of workers as a cost-cutting measure," the report added.

The report said that reforms also helped erase coffee identity in some areas. It said coffee processed and sold from specific villages was no longer possible because a rush to get to the market meant processors mixed everything they got.

The report said the purchasing power of the unions was declining while that of private buyers rose. It said unions found it difficult to pay farmers because local commercial banks were reluctant to give them overdraft facilities.
